"Parallel" describes two or more things that run alongside each other, always staying the same distance apart, never getting closer and never drifting farther away — no matter how far they extend.

That last part is crucial. It's not just about being next to each other. It's about maintaining that exact, unchanging gap, forever.

Imagine two straight roads running through a vast, open desert. They never bend toward each other. They never bend away. They just stretch on and on, side by side, with the same gap between them at every single point. Those roads are parallel.

The classic example is railway tracks. The two rails run alongside each other from one city to another — always the same distance apart, never touching. They are parallel lines.

What makes something not parallel?

  • If the two roads eventually meet at a point (like the letter V), they are converging — not parallel.
  • If they start close together and slowly spread apart (like the letter ∧ flipped), they are diverging — not parallel.
  • If one road curves while the other stays straight — not parallel.

Parallel means: same direction, same distance, always. No meeting. No separating.

This applies not just to lines but to surfaces, planes, and any spatial forms. Two walls of a corridor are parallel to each other. The top and bottom edges of a door are parallel. The floors of a building are parallel planes.
The Figurative Meaning (and This Is Where It Gets Rich)

Language borrowed this geometric idea and stretched it beautifully into non-physical territory. When something in real life "runs alongside" something else — in terms of structure, pattern, or timing — we call it parallel too.

Here, "parallel" takes on two overlapping senses:

1. Corresponding or Similar in Nature

When two things share a similar structure, pattern, or nature — even if they exist in completely different contexts — they are said to be parallel.

"The two countries went through parallel struggles after independence."

This means: both countries went through struggles that were remarkably similar in shape and pattern — perhaps both dealt with economic hardship, political instability, and social unrest, in a similar sequence. The struggles didn't literally run next to each other in space; but when you look at them side by side, they mirror each other, the way two railway tracks mirror each other.

More examples:

  • "She was reading the book while her son drew pictures — parallel activities that kept them both busy."

Here, "parallel" means the two activities happened in a comparable, side-by-side fashion — each person doing their own thing, independently, at the same time.

  • "There is a parallel between the rise of the Roman Empire and the rise of the British Empire."

The word "parallel" here means: a notable similarity in pattern, course of events, or structure.

  • "He led a parallel life — a quiet professor by day, a jazz musician by night."

This means he lived two separate lives simultaneously, one alongside the other, with little overlap.

2. Happening at the Same Time (Simultaneously)

"Parallel" is also used to describe things that happen at the same time, especially when they are separate but related processes happening alongside each other.

"The two teams conducted parallel investigations into the same crime."

This means: both teams were investigating independently, at the same time, following similar or identical procedures — like two tracks running side by side.

"The software runs parallel processes to complete the task faster."

In computing, "parallel" is used heavily. Instead of doing task 1, then task 2, then task 3 (one after another), a system that runs things in parallel does task 1, task 2, and task 3 all at the same time, simultaneously.
The Key Quality That Ties All Meanings Together

In every use of "parallel" — spatial, figurative, or simultaneous — there is one unifying idea:

Two or more things exist or occur side by side, independently of each other, without merging into one thing, without colliding, and without diverging into completely different territory.

They remain distinct. They remain comparable. And they maintain that relationship consistently.

It helps to see how "parallel" differs from words that might seem related:

  • Similar just means two things share some qualities. But "parallel" implies a deeper structural resemblance — the pattern or course is alike, not just a few features.
  • Simultaneous just means two things happen at the same time. "Parallel" adds the idea that they are also comparable or running along a similar path — not just coincidentally occurring together.
  • Identical means the same thing. "Parallel" things are not the same thing — they are separate things that correspond to each other.

• A parallel situation — a situation that closely mirrors another in structure or outcome.
  • Draw a parallel (or draw parallels) — to point out a similarity between two things. "The historian drew a parallel between the two wars."
  • Run parallel to — to exist alongside something in a similar manner. "His career ran parallel to his brother's for many years."
  • In parallel — simultaneously, alongside each other. "The two experiments were conducted in parallel."
  • A parallel universe — a universe that exists alongside ours, with its own separate but (possibly) similar reality. This is where the word finds its most imaginative use.

Parallel (adjective) describes things — lines, events, processes, lives, stories — that:

  1. Run alongside each other in space, in time, or in pattern,
  2. Stay consistently comparable without merging or sharply diverging, and
  3. Remain distinct from each other.

The spatial image of two railway tracks that never meet, never drift apart, and go on forever — that is the soul of this word. Every figurative use is an echo of that image.
